questions.q: What does the CIA triad stand for in data security?
options: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability
Collection, Identification, Access
Consent, Information, Accountability
Classification, Inventory, Audit
questions.explain: The CIA triad is the standard model for data security: confidentiality (only authorized access), integrity (accurate, untampered data), and availability (accessible to legitimate users when needed).

questions.q: Which of these is a direct identifier rather than a quasi-identifier?
options: A 5-digit ZIP code
A full date of birth
A Social Security number
A gender field
questions.explain: A Social Security number identifies a specific person on its own. ZIP code, birth date, and gender are quasi-identifiers â€” each is shared by many people, but together they can narrow a dataset down to one person.

questions.q: GDPR applies to the personal data of people in the EU based on which factor?
options: Where the person whose data it is is located, regardless of where the processing organization is based
Only where the processing organization has a registered EU office
Only to data stored on servers physically located in the EU
Only to companies with more than 500 EU employees
questions.explain: GDPR has extraterritorial scope: it protects EU residents' personal data no matter where the organization processing it is headquartered.

questions.q: Who developed Privacy by Design and its 7 Foundational Principles?
options: Ann Cavoukian, former Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, Canada
A working group within the European Commission
The US Department of Health and Human Services
The PCAOB
questions.explain: Ann Cavoukian, while serving as Ontario's Information and Privacy Commissioner, developed Privacy by Design and its 7 Foundational Principles.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is data classification?
options: Sorting data into sensitivity tiers so handling rules can apply consistently and automatically
Encrypting every dataset in an organization at the same strength
Deleting data once it reaches a certain age
A legal requirement that only applies to healthcare organizations
questions.explain: Classification assigns a sensitivity label to data so that access, encryption, retention, and sharing rules attach automatically, instead of being decided case by case.

questions.q: In the common four-tier commercial classification scheme described in this lesson, which tier is described as fine for anyone, inside or outside the organization, to see?
options: Public
Internal
Confidential
Restricted
questions.explain: Public covers information like marketing material or published pricing â€” there's no harm in anyone seeing it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say organizations often have sensitive data that has never been classified?
options: Because classification schemes don't apply to spreadsheets or log files
Because that data was never discovered in the first place â€” nobody knew it existed to classify it
Because classification is legally optional in every jurisdiction
Because sensitive data automatically deletes itself after a set period
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that you can't classify what you haven't found â€” old exports, forgotten spreadsheets, backups, and log files often hold sensitive data nobody inventoried.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is access governance, as distinct from the individual controls in this chapter?
options: The program that decides when each control fires, who's accountable, and how grants are proven correct later
A single software product that replaces all other access controls
A one-time project completed when a company is founded
A synonym for role-based access control
questions.explain: Access governance is the coordinating layer: it schedules and documents controls like RBAC, least privilege, SoD, reviews, and privileged-access management rather than being a separate control itself.

questions.q: What is the core idea of role-based access control as described in this lesson?
options: Permissions attach to roles, and roles attach to people, instead of granting permissions to individuals one at a time
Every user gets administrator access by default
Permissions are granted based on an employee's physical office location
Access is granted only once per calendar year regardless of role changes
questions.explain: RBAC splits the problem into defining what a role needs and deciding who holds that role, so a change to the role's permissions propagates to every member automatically.

questions.q: Which statement best matches this lesson's definition of least privilege?
options: Every account gets the minimum access required for its job â€” nothing added for convenience or kept 'just in case'
Every account should have administrator access to avoid future access requests
Access should be granted once and never reviewed again
Only the most senior employees should have any system access at all
questions.explain: Least privilege is the narrowing principle: for every permission, you should be able to name the specific task that requires it.

questions.q: What question does segregation of duties (SoD) ask, as distinguished from least privilege in this lesson?
options: Can one person, alone, complete an entire sensitive process end to end?
Does this one account have too much access for its job?
How often should passwords be changed?
Which encryption algorithm should protect data at rest?
questions.explain: Least privilege scopes a single account's permissions; SoD asks whether a whole sensitive process can be completed, start to finish, by one person alone.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish data masking from encryption?
options: Masking hides values from a query's results without changing the stored data; encryption protects data from anyone without the right key, including raw file access
Masking and encryption are two names for the exact same technique
Masking only works on numeric columns, while encryption only works on text columns
Encryption is reversible by anyone, while masking is never reversible
questions.explain: Masking's threat model is a legitimate, authenticated user who shouldn't see a column's true value; encryption protects against someone who doesn't hold the decryption key at all, including at the storage layer.

questions.q: Which three points in a data's lifecycle does this lesson identify as needing encryption?
options: At rest, in transit, and in use
At creation, at deletion, and at backup only
Only at rest â€” the other two don't apply to databases
Only in transit â€” data at rest never needs protection
questions.explain: The lesson covers data sitting on disk (at rest), moving across a network (in transit, via TLS), and being actively processed in memory (in use).

questions.q: Per this lesson, where do most real-world encryption failures actually occur?
options: In how the key is handled across its lifetime, not in the underlying cryptographic math
In the mathematical algorithms themselves, which are usually broken
Only in the choice of programming language used
Encryption failures are almost always caused by network latency
questions.explain: The lesson states the cryptography is sound; failures come from mishandling the key â€” poor storage, no rotation, over-sharing, or loss.

questions.q: How does this lesson's column-level GRANT example implement least privilege?
options: GRANT accepts a specific column list, so HRRole and PayrollRole each see only the exact columns their role needs, nothing else
It grants every role access to every column by default
It requires a separate masking function for every column
It only works on numeric columns, never on text columns
questions.explain: GRANT SELECT ON dbo.Employees(EmployeeId, Name, Department) TO HRRole scopes the role to exactly those columns, with Salary granted separately and only to PayrollRole.

questions.q: What is the main risk of over-retention?
options: It increases breach exposure by keeping data around long after any legitimate need
It makes storage too cheap to justify
It automatically violates every retention schedule
It has no real downside since storage is inexpensive
questions.explain: Every extra year data sits in a system is another year it can be breached, must be secured, and may be subject to erasure requests â€” the exposure, not the storage cost, is the real risk.

questions.q: What is a 'soft delete'?
options: Flagging a record as deleted without physically removing it from storage
Permanently overwriting the underlying storage so data is unrecoverable
A type of encryption applied before deletion
A legal term for an erasure request that was denied
questions.explain: A soft delete sets a flag like is_deleted = true. The row is still physically present and still readable by anyone with direct database or backup access.

questions.q: What distinguishes a true audit trail from a system that merely 'has logs'?
options: An audit trail is specifically built to answer who did what, to which data, when, and with what outcome
An audit trail only records failed actions, never successful ones
An audit trail is any log file regardless of its content
An audit trail is generated exclusively by the database engine
questions.explain: Generic logs (errors, timings) don't necessarily capture attributable identity, specific resources touched, or outcomes â€” an audit trail is purpose-built to answer those five questions.

questions.q: In the breach response lifecycle, why does containment come before full assessment?
options: Waiting until the incident is fully understood would let the exposure continue, so stopping it takes priority even with an imperfect picture
Containment is actually the last step in the lifecycle, not an early one
Assessment is unnecessary once containment is complete
Regulations require containment to happen exactly 72 hours after detection
questions.explain: The lifecycle accepts an imperfect early picture in exchange for stopping the ongoing exposure immediately, rather than waiting for full clarity before acting.

questions.q: In the Brightfield Retail scenario, how was the contractor's database access originally granted?
options: By role-copying â€” mirroring another team's permissions â€” instead of scoping access to the actual dashboard task
Through a formal least-privilege review scoped to the dashboard task
It was never granted at all, which was the actual failure
Through a one-time, automatically expiring temporary credential
questions.explain: Access was granted as 'give them what the analytics team has' rather than scoped to what the dashboard work actually required â€” a classic role-copying failure covered in Chapter 3.
